bib.title: Has It All Been Solved? Open NLP Research Questions Not Solved by Large Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Has It All Been Solved? Open NLP Research Questions Not Solved by Large Language Models", Oana Ignat*, Zhijing Jin*, Rada Mihalcea and ~20 co-authors (Univ. of Michigan LIT lab). arXiv 2305.12544v2, 15 Mar 2024; position paper, cs.CL. The header/keywords format suggests LREC-COLING 2024, but the extraction does not say so; treat venue as "preprint". First version was May 2023.

COVERAGE: All 45 pages, 203,170 chars. I read the full body (about chars 0-46,800), the appendix, and the start of the bibliography. I skimmed the rest of the references (about 150k chars) for origins only. Text extraction is clean apart from harmless pypdf float warnings. The PDF contains no embedded instructions.

BOTTOM LINE: This is a research-agenda or opinion survey. It has no experiments, no results tables and no benchmarks. The only numbers are counts of its own taxonomy, and it makes no checkable quantitative claim of its own. It cites other work for a few numbers but quotes none of them. It maps only loosely to the notes in generative-ai/01-llm-fundamentals/notes/. The nearest are 05 (hallucination), 03 and 15 (scale and cost), 07 and 09 (SFT, PEFT) and 10 (prompting). It fits best as a "what LLMs still don't do" framing citation, not as evidence.

CLAIMS (ranked; the only numbers are taxonomy counts)
- claim: The authors list 14 research areas with 45 directions that they say LLMs do not directly solve.
  number: 14 areas, 45 directions
  setup: Taxonomy from a sticky-note brainstorm in one US academic lab (LIT). It is not a systematic survey.
  quote: "We identify fourteen different research areas encompassing 45 research directions that require new research and are not directly solvable by LLMs."
  where: Abstract, p.1
- claim: The areas were chosen to be thesis-sized, free of paid-API dependence and affordable in an academic lab.
  number: none
  setup: Three stated selection principles, plus the ACL 2018 area list.
  quote: "building systems that cannot function without paid APIs is not well aligned with academic core research goals."
  where: Sec 1, p.2
- claim: The list covers 15 of the 21 ACL 2018 areas.
  number: 15/21
  setup: Appendix Table 1 maps areas to ACL tracks. The excluded ones are said to be within LLM purview (Summarization, Syntax and Parsing, Discourse, and others) or outside the authors' expertise.
  quote: "from which we select the ones not in the purview of LLMs (15/21 areas)"
  where: Sec 1; Appendix Table 1
- claim: Next-word prediction can reward invalid reasoning, and fully supervised training on correct reasoning demonstrations does not fix it. Scaling helps, but prompting is still needed to elicit correct reasoning.
  number: none
  setup: Cited work (Khalifa et al. 2023; Uesato et al. 2022; Wei et al. 2022c), not tested here.
  quote: "the next-word prediction objective can easily encourage the LM to assign a high likelihood to invalid reasoning (Khalifa et al., 2023). Even fully-supervised training over correct reasoning demonstrations does not solve the issue (Uesato et al., 2022)."
  where: Sec 2.2, p.2
- claim: LLMs are not equally good across languages. The authors blame training-data proportions and annotator demographics in RLHF. They also say general-purpose LLMs trail dedicated MT models.
  number: none
  setup: Cites OpenAI 2023, Huang et al. 2023a, Ahuja et al. 2023 (MEGA). Dated to early 2023 models.
  quote: "At present, general-purpose LLMs do not perform as well as models trained specifically for translation"
  where: Sec 2.1, p.2
- claim: Hallucination remains an issue even with retrieval or tools, and LLMs alone are not sufficient for fact-checking. Proposed mitigations are references and sources, external KB lookup, and tool use (calculators, search).
  number: none
  setup: Cites Ji et al. 2022, Dziri et al. 2022, Schick et al. 2023 and others.
  quote: "LLMs are prone to hallucinations (Dziri et al., 2022b; Raunak et al., 2021) and factual inconsistencies (Tam et al., 2023), so they might not be self-sufficient to combat misinformation reliably."
  where: Sec 3.4, p.4
- claim: LLM annotation is partial. Few-shot and zero-shot models are often beaten by models fine-tuned on human labels, and ChatGPT has higher recall than precision (more false positives).
  number: none (qualitative)
  setup: Reported from Ollion et al. 2023, not measured here. Applies to computational social science labelling tasks.
  quote: "Ollion et al. (2023) show that few-shot and zero-shot models are often outperformed by models fine-tuned with human annotations. Additionally, ChatGPT usually yields higher recall than precision"
  where: Sec 4.3, p.5
- claim: Data deduplication and curation methods are lacking at very large corpus scale.
  number: ">700B tokens" (the authors' threshold)
  setup: Sec 3.3, stated without a source for the threshold.
  quote: "there is a lack of effective methods for data deduplication and curation for vast corpora (>700B Tokens) or raw web data used for training very big models."
  where: Sec 3.3, p.4
- claim: LLMs need far more data than children, so child-language-acquisition research could improve sample efficiency.
  number: none
  setup: Opinion, citing Warstadt et al. 2023 (BabyLM) and Linzen 2020.
  quote: "LLMs require far more data than children to acquire language, and LLMs can be improved in sample efficiency by learning how children acquire language."
  where: Sec 2.5, p.3
- claim: Multimodal fusion is unsolved, since modalities can compete and many uni-modal models outperform multi-modal ones. Multimodal LLMs were limited to text, audio and visual.
  number: none
  setup: As of 2023; this has likely dated.
  quote: "in some cases, modalities end up competing with each other (Yao and Mihalcea, 2022), and thus many uni-modal models outperform multi-modal models"
  where: Sec 2.4, p.3
- claim: Other directions the paper lists:
  - Reasoning evaluation is hard because of data contamination, Goodhart's law and a lack of metrics for multi-step reasoning.
  - Efficiency work covers attention (Dao 2022, which is FlashAttention), MoE (Fedus 2021) and PEFT (prompt-tuning by Lester 2021; Hu 2023 for LoRA-style methods).
  - Distillation moved from soft logits (Hinton 2015) to LLM-generated synthetic examples (West 2022; Alpaca/Taori 2023).
  - Interpretability: probing and mechanistic work.
  number: none
  quote: "how to test a model's reasoning skills in the face of data contamination, Goodhart's law (a dataset failing to reflect the skill once exploited) ... and a lack of reliable metrics to evaluate multi-step reasoning"
  where: Sec 2.2, p.2

LIMITS
- The authors concede it is not exhaustive: "many others exist". It leaves out areas where LLMs lag (information extraction, QA, summarization) and all LLM-development research.
- No methodology beyond a lab brainstorm. The authors are from a single lab, and the paper says so ("members of an academic NLP research lab in the United States").
- Directions are described briefly and are not evaluated ("did not aim to solve any of the tasks").
- It is dated to early-2023 capabilities (ChatGPT, GPT-4 era). The 2024 revision only added a few citations. Claims such as "no LLMs combine gesture with text" and "multimodal LLMs limited to text, audio, visual" are stale by 2026. Reasoning-model results (o1 and later) post-date it.
- The "LLMs can't do X" claims rest on cited papers, not on anything run here.

BUILDS ON: Shannon 1948 (n-gram or Markov language models); Brown et al. 1988 and Jelinek 1976 (statistical MT and speech); Hinton et al. 2015 (distillation); Bang et al. 2023a (ChatGPT evaluation, where LLMs lag); Wei et al. 2022 (chain of thought); Schick et al. 2023 (Toolformer); Ouyang et al. 2022 (InstructGPT/RLHF); the ACL 2018 area list.

CODE: none.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.1): the 14 research areas, grouped as Fundamental / Responsible / Applied. It is the whole taxonomy at a glance.
- Fig 2 (p.5): "What should I work on?" decision map by motivation. It has no data.
- Appendix Table 1: area to ACL 2018 track mapping.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Nothing numeric to verify beyond taxonomy counts; I did not check any cited papers' numbers.
- The venue is not printed in the extraction, only the arXiv stamp.
- Note for mapping: my grep of note 05 shows it already cites Ortega 2021, Zhang 2023 and the InstructGPT hallucination result. This paper adds no number to that. It could only "sharpen" the claim that hallucination persists and that tools or retrieval are proposed mitigations (Sec 2.3 and 3.4), as a citation plus a references row.
